projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Richard Koepke was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Good morning, today's date is November 11, 2011. My name is Emily Lee. I'm conducting an oral history interview at Prince Institute in Schaumburg, Illinois, with Richard Koepke. All right. So, I have a list of questions here, but if there's anything that you want to talk about that I'm not asking, feel free to, you know -

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: Just ask anything you want.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Okay, so first can we just talk about how you got into the service? Were you drafted, or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: I was 18. I had just graduated from high school; now, this would be 1940. I had joined the Illinois National Guard April 10, 1940. The reason I joined the National Guard is there was talk about the war possibility. And my father had been in WWI. My step-father was also in The National Guard at the time, and he was my dad's First Sargent; and that's where he met my mother. After my dad died - my dad died as a result of being gassed in WWI. His death certificate says Tuberculosis, but when he was in service, as they say, he was attached to the Australian Army. He was in an attack and they were gassed, and he reported to the British Military Hospital. Of course, there's no record of that being in the United States. And so, when he was discharged, he became a captain in the Army and in the National Guard. He died in 1925. I was four and a half or five at the time. My mother married my step-father after that, and because of what my mother knew and what my step-father knew, at the time, we were probably going to get into - involved in the war. So, I had signed up because I was still familiar with the military. I joined the Illinois National Guard April 10, 1940. The Ohio National Guard had been federalized in October of 1940, and so we knew we were going to get federalized sometime afterward. On March 5, 1941, I was - we were federalized. I am the 7568th soldier from the Illinois National Guard that was federalized and that's how I got involved with the military. We went down to Camp Forrest, at the time the Illinois National Guard 33rd Division went down to camp in Tellahoma, Tennessee, Camp Forrest. And it was an experience. I got promoted to Sargent at the time and when the war broke out, December 7, 1941. I was fortunate, if you want to call it that, to be Company Duty Sargent at the time. So I was involved with that day, somewhat. Being Duty Sargent at the time, I could not leave that weekend. I could not leave the camp area. I was Senior Sargent in Charge of whatever when on that day so I was in the - gotten up and had breakfast on that Sunday and I was in my quarters reading the newspaper, Sunday paper. All the sudden I heard some racket out in the squad room and I went out there and said "What's going on?" The Japs bombed Pearl Harbor. I said, "No, they didn't. I said you're talking about Australia or something else. No, no, no." And just then the company orderly, the times, come running for me and said "The Lieutenant wants you." So, I went to the orderly room. The Lieutenant Senior Officer of the day was there. He told me, get everybody in camp, full field pack and get ready to move. So I gave orders to all the troops that were in camp. He also told me to get the full field packs ready to move out that night. When we - he told me to get the kitchen equipment ready, start getting the machine gun belts loaded with ammunition, BAR magazines loaded with ammunition and get ready to move out. So, as the other troops, company members coming back in eventually a full company was formed and we were ready to move out.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: How did you feel during all that? Were you nervous? Excited?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: It was excitement, just excitement. Everything was chaotic; nobody knew what was going on. We were waiting for orders, since nobody knew what was going on. Across the parade ground was the artillery units, coast artillery, field artillery units and so forth and so on. They moved out. Our coast artillery units moved out of camp that night for the west coast. We stayed on alert for a period of time, things calmed down by the next day a little bit. A week later we were assigned duties to guard the powerhouses and dams and so forth and so on in Chattanooga, Tennessee. After that, shortly after that, President Roosevelt made the announcement that he wanted to have 50,000 air craft. They were going to build 50,000 air craft, they needed pilots. So I transferred, put in my request to be transferred to the Air Corps because I decided I wanted to be a pilot. I wanted to fly. And fortunately, again fortunately, I was excepted and probably a week or two after I was excepted into the Air Corps, now the Air Corps belonged to the Army at that time. I was excepted to the Air Corps and the transfer papers were going to come through. The other regiment, the 132nd - I was in the 131st Infantry Regiment, the 132nd Infantry Regiment was alerted to go to the South Pacific. And they transferred men from the 131st into the 132nd Infantry to bring the 132nd up to full strength and they shipped out to the South Pacific. Those that I knew that came back from the South Pacific all came back with some kind of fungus disease or something. As I say, I was lucky. I couldn't go. I was transferred to the Air Corps. So I went - they didn't know what to do with me now. So, they gave me a 90-day furlough waiting for my orders to go - to come down. My orders eventually came and I got transferred down to Craig Field, Selma, Alabama.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Now, at this time were you married or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: No, no, no, I was single. I was a Sargent at the time. But I was single; I wasn't interested in getting married because, primarily because of what happened to my father. You know, I didn't want to tie any girl up with coming back from war with some kind of battle injury and so forth.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: So military was a your priority? Did you join more out of tribute to your dad, or do you feel it was your duty to, or you wanted to be a part of ir?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: Again, you gotta remember in 1940 a dollar was a lot of money. I graduated from high school. I had been working after school in a fruit market and getting maybe a dollar a day or something like that. A dollar was a lot of money, and because of being warned that we were gonna get involved in a war, I joined. Because of that reason and plus I could get some money. In other words, when we went to drill every week we got paid a dollar a day. We got paid every three months. So, at that particular time $13 together in one lump sum was a lot of money. And that was another reason, that I could have some money. From the time I worked in grammar school I always had to give the money I earned to my mother for whatever. She would always give me 25 percent of what I gave her. So the rest of the money was for clothes and whatnot. $13 was a lot of money.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Did you go through a boot camp or training when you first enter in.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: We were trained in the National Guard, and then after we got federalized, I was doing the training because I had learned basic military protocol.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: And you were young when you were in charge of all these people. Were they the same age as you, or older? How did that work?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: As they say, I learned a lot. Because when we got federalized, shortly after that, the draft started, or just before that the draft started and we started to get our first draftees. A lot of our draftees were older than we were. A lot of the draftees were married, and we were taught that being in command of a group of men, responsible for a group of men, to take care of them. So, we heard many of their problems. So, me, being a 19-year-old kid telling married people what they should do to solve their marriage problems. Now, what did I know.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: How were the draftees' attitudes coming in? Did you have anybody that was really difficult?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: No, we didn't. They were being drafted. Back then, when the war started, it was our duty. We had a job to do. The country called us to do a job and most of us, of the men, came down there with that attitude. We had a job to do. They had to learn.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: I guess we can talk about your first deployment. How you got the orders to go overseas, the first time, and can you tell us about that.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: My first deployment, I had washed out of the Air Corps. I had passed all the physical tests from the Air Corps, and they transferred me to Santa Ana Air Base which was an Aviation Cadet Training School. I was going to be a cadet. I passed all the tests there except one. They presented to me the Japanese color chart. I am totally color-blind. Totally color-blind means I that can't see shades. I can tell red, blue, green and so on and so forth. So, because of that condition they washed me out and they offered me different things in the Air Force. I decided because of my military training in the Army and in the Infantry, I didn't like the Air Force because they were too lax. They didn't have any military protocol; so, I said no. They offered me to be a bombardier; they offered me to be a navigator. I wanted to be a pilot, and I didn't want to be a bomber. I wanted to fly. I was going to be a pursuit pilot. Anyway, I wanted to go back into the Infantry. Ultimately, they transferred me back the Infantry Officers Candidate School, Fort Bend, Georgia, and I became a 90-day wonder, became a 2nd Lieutenant. From there they transferred me to the 42nd Calvary because the 42nd Infantry Division was being reorganized, recalled. They were the famous rainbow division from WWI. I was part of the calvary, and I was there for nine months, and I got shipment orders for overseas duty. So, from there I went to Newport News, Virginia. It took us 28 days to go by ship to Naples, Italy. That was a long time. MS. Lee: What was that like? Maybe exciting for the first two days and then it was long? What did you do with your time?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: What was on the ship?

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Yes?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: Okay. We were on a Liberty Ship. Liberty Ships were build in sections. There was the bow, the middle, and the stern. And they were put together, assembled someplace else, brought together, and welded up. So, and had five holds in them. Where you put the equipment. On the ship there were 550 enlisted men and 50 officers, being shipped in separate groups. They were loaded in the two metal, we were stored in the two metal holds. The front hold was primarily for crew. We were in the middle two sections of the ship. The first ship hold was primarily for the crew. The back two holds, the fourth and the fifth, one of them was loaded with artillery and ammunition. The other hold was loaded with ton and a half trucks filled with gasoline. Five days out of Newport News, we hit a storm. And everybody got seasick. Because not being used to - and the odor from the gasoline fumes made everybody seasick. And then, after we were on the ship and we went through the storm, about 10 days maybe 15 days out in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean they found out that the ship was beginning to split apart. And about five-feet down the side of the ship and five- across the deck and so we had to fall out of the convoy because there's nobody on the ship that knows how to weld. So, we fell out of our convoy. Our convoy was probably a 50-ship convoy, and so, we had to fall out of the convoy while the rest of the convoy went ahead. The Navy sent a crew aboard ship to weld up the side of the ship, and we were out there alone wondering whether the submarines are out there or not. And they welded us back up and eventually we caught up to the convoy. And I had learned that when I get aboard a ship, to start eating crackers. That's what I do.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: So then, from Italy, where did you go? MR, KOEPKE: We landed in Naples, Italy. In the Mediterranean, going through the Straights of Gibraltar was an experience. I happen to get up on deck early in the morning and this 50 ship convoy had disappeared on each side of us and the ships were in front of us and I watched the ships in front of me. It was like Jonah was being swallowed by the whale. That's just the way it felt to me, that ship was there and then it disappeared. The description that I gave my mother about the Straights of Gibraltar was that it was like a huge rock was put in the middle of a puddle, and we ultimately ended up in Naples, Italy.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Naples is the southern most point?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: No. It's in the middle of Italy, on the western side.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: And then once you docked there, what happened?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: That was a surprise. MR.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: What did you expect to happen?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: My introduction to Italy, we pulled into the harbor and saw the all these people on the docks. They were going to welcome us, were they? No. What they were waiting for was for our ship to unload the garbage and they would go through it to find out anything they could use. Believe it or not. The ships didn't throw the garbage overboard these 28 days. They kept it in a hold someplace. That was unbelievable.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: To use for their day to day lives or they thought military information was in there.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: No. Something to eat. Something they could use. While I was in Italy, in Naples, I went to a replacement depot, and we were waiting for assignment for one of the battle groups on the front lines. And because of whatever was going on in front in the battles that were going on in the other places in Italy. We didn't get called up right away, breaking our boredom we got, I was fortunate again to get assigned to MP duty in Naples. The assignment of the MP duties in Naples was to break up the black market groups. Because black market pilfering and stealing from the Italians and even the military was rampant. There must have been 20 officers, and what duties we were assigned to was we were riding shotgun on convoys. We would take a three or four truck convoy of supplies from the dock to the quarter master depot and so forth and we'd be on, riding shotgun for these trucks because what would happen is the Italian Mafia or whoever would pull a donkey cart in front of the trucks to stop them. The minute they stopped people would jump out and throw stuff off the trucks or they'd take - Italy at that time, streets were narrow, trucks slow down and people would jump off the balconies into the back of the truck and throw stuff off - the streets were made of cobblestone, big stones, they'd pull these out so the trucks would stop and our job was to prevent it and we carried a tommy gum and we'd spray the area. Our quarters were, they put us in bombed out hotels in downtown Naples and we were down there a couple of times and the harbor was bombed, and so forth and so on. I had too much to drink one night and I didn't care what was going on. I wasn't gonna move out of the bed. I just couldn't move anymore.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: So, were you still excited at that point or were you getting scared.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: I don't know. I ask myself, was I ever scared? I don't know. It's, I think my training always took over. It was a job to do and this - whatever happened, happened. The one time that I remember being scared was the day the Korean War broke out. We were back in the National Guard this was 1953 or '54. We were, the national guard had been training at Camp McCoy at the time and the Korean War broke out and I got scared. I didn't want to do this again. I'd already been through a war and that's my feeling of being scared. I wanted to go run and hide someplace. I'd done this before. I had spent six years in the middle, and I didn't want to do this anymore. So, prior to that I don't think I was scared. We had a job to do, and we were supposed to do it. Now, that's the way I felt.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: So when you got called up in Italy.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: After Naples, I got assigned to the 3rd Infantry Division and I joined the 3rd Division right after they broke out of Anzio. They broke out of Anzio, if I remember correctly, 25th of May. They started breaking up, and I joined them on the 1st of June. I was in Naples, or not Naples, I was in Rome the day they landed at Normandy. We garrisoned in Rome for about five or ten days. And we got pulled back to train for the invasion of Southern France. We got pulled back to Naples to train for the invasion of Southern France. It's difficult to explain what I'm going to explain. I don't understand it. The battle, Anzio battlefield, the troops had moved out. They had gone towards Rome. The battlefield, there was no battle going on, understand, and that's when I landed in Anzio. The, I felt something when I passed through the battlefield. I don't know today what I felt. I would call it, I could call it the feeling of death. I could call it the stillness of death. I could call it the touch of death. It was quiet. It was so still. There was no noise, even though these military trucks were there. I didn't hear any noise. There was no breeze, but there was. No birds. It had a smell like fresh air, only it wasn't fresh air. I felt something. I felt that two other times. I felt it another time when I was in a concentration camp in Dachau, Germany. I felt it again when I visited a Holocaust Museum in Washington DC. The same feeling that surrounded me. It's hard to explain. I couldn't put in it writing, and occasionally, I'll feel it at a funeral, especially at one of my relatives. It's a comfortable feeling, but it's a feeling I don't like.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: I think you explain it well.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: It's different, and the air, there's no air but you're breathing. Just different. Anyway we went to, after we trained near Naples for the battle of the invasion of Southern France, we landed in the southern part of France. I was in the second assault wave. I get annoyed, irritated, upset, every time I hear about what happened in Normandy. I think it was uncalled for. The Army and the Navy and the Air Force, in my opinion, they didn't do their job correctly in Normandy. We were - I wrote a letter home on the invasion of Southern France to my mother, and everything happened the way it was suppose to happen when we landed on the beaches of Southern France. We advanced up the Rhine River Valley to secure towns and liberate towns in the area, beautiful country right there. We saw the, took part in the destruction of the German Army at Montpelier, France. We almost destroyed the entire 19th German Army at that time, but they got away. Destruction there was awful. We crossed the Vogues Mountains in France - went to cross - there went into Strasbourg, France, liberated that and went down into Colmar area which was suppose to be secured or liberated by the French Army, but they couldn't do it. The 3rd Division went down there and did most of the fighting down there. We got the Presidential Unit Citation with Oak Leaf Cluster.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Can you describe what maybe your day-to-day life was like when you - you were in combat at that time. What the actual fighting was like.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: I don't remember. I can tell you this; I was cold all the time. I didn't have enough sleep. We were constantly on the go. We fought in the mountains. I don't remember battles. I try to remember what I did in the various battles, but I don't remember. As hard as I try. I can remember burning down houses. I can remember people I didn't kill. For example, we had taken a town, liberated, captured, taken a town and the strong point of the town was a house and I went into the house and heard some noise down in the basement. Now, we'd been fighting there and I found a trap door down in the basement and I was getting ready to throw in a hand grenade and just then I heard some kid's voice. And that's the were it happened in a house or area where we're staying while the battle was going on. Another incident we were in a battle and I saw an enemy soldier running away and I had just finished firing a last shot out of my rifle that I cared. He was running away, an MG42 machine gun with him and I pulled out my pistol to shoot him and it wouldn't go off because it had froze. I can tell you that, but I can't tell you anything about the battles.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: How did you get your orders of where to go next?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: Verbally. I mean, you know, we didn't - the captain got the orders and our job was to carry them out. I mean that's the way we did things. The 3rd Division as a whole at the end of the war has the most decorations, has the most casualties of the war. I knew, am familiar with, talked to, fought with, to with various medal of honer winners. I knew Audie Murphy. He and I were on leave once together. Other medals of honor, I saw them happen. Battles, how they were awarded and what they were awarded the metal of honor for. I don't remember having a battle. There's so much - it was a good experience.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: In during that time in France, were some of your men killed or did you have casualties? How was that Handled?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: Let's put it this way. I'll give you statistics. When we landed at Southern France on the beach at St Tropes, there were 200 men in the company. We were in the mountains in September, October we were at probably almost half strength. We got very few replacements. When the cold battle in Chaumont ended, which was the end of February, we had 58 men in our company. There were 200 men which included officers. There's six officers in every company. The captain and I were the only two office left. And we had 58 men. We got replacements. Generally, when you got replacements after the first battle, you lost at least 50 percent of them. Because they didn't have the training that they needed.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Probably not used to the elements.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: One time when we were advancing up, we were moving so fast and chasing the Germans so fast up the Rhine River, transportation - our ammunition couldn't keep up with us, and we used, instead of using artillery in attacks to help support our attack, we had to use mortars which - see we weren't getting replacements. So, we had to do what we had to do and because of the training and the experience of the 3rd division we were successful. One time I had gotten - I had probably 15 men in my platoon at the time and there should have been 40. I had gotten eight men as replacements. We went into the battle and I lost three of them. So that's, you know.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: And how did you handle that personally? You probably didn't have time or energy to dwell; you just kept going?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: We just went on, you just had to ignore it. I had written a letter toward the end of the war to my mother and the war, I was telling her, the war was almost over and I'd be coming home and I had changed so much. How am I going to handle the situation with today? The people in the states don't know what this is all about. How am I going to act? How are people going to react to me? And I might have been homesick that day. I was just rambling on in this letter. To straighten things. I mean. You know I talked about the husbands' wives and their husbands. You know, I feel sorry for the guys today. We didn't have the pressure that they are on. I can't imagine them with technology today, calling home on a cell phone in the morning to kids or wives then goes out on a mission and then comes back and talking the kids again, what he thinks about. While we didn't hear. We didn't have that outside contact. I just - we didn't have my contact with home. One time, it was three weeks before I got any mail. It was frequently 10-15 days before I got any news from home. Why? Because we were in battle. And what had priority was ammunition and food, mail didn't count. We didn't have that stress. I never thought of getting killed, we didn't, that was part of the job. So, what their going through today with the technology; it's not the same. We knew who we were fighting, they don't.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Right now we're talking about your time in France. Can you talk about the transitions to when you All went into Germany?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: The battle of Colmar Pocket ended in February. The Division was pulled out of line to reorganize. At that particular time, I got transferred. There were a lot of transfers. I got transferred out of a line company which at that time was K company which was a rifle company into an anti-tank company. The captain in the company got sent back to the United States. Audie Murphy, who happened to be in the Division, he got transferred out of the company into headquarters. I got lucky. I got transferred to an anti-tank company. I was no longer on the front line. At that particular time, the threat from Germany armored was diminished. They didn't need an anti-tank company as such. As a member of an anti-tank company - an anti-tank company consisted of three platoons, vehicles, and large anti-tank guns. Generally, all the way through Germany, we got special assignments. At one time, we liberated Augsberg. They didn't want to fight there. The mayor didn't want the town to be destroyed. So my platoon, we were given the job of clearing out the underground sewer system which they were using for bomb shelters. We had to go in there and check to make sure there were no enemy soldiers in there, and that was kind of scary at the time, because it was dark. There's no lights except for candles or lanterns all the way through the underground system that they had there, and it was kind if scary when we went through it. Another time we were given an assignment to act as a guard of a POW camp which had 8,000 Germans in it for a while. We did that for a period of time until the regular military police came up and took over.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: What was that like, guarding that POW camp.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: The camp was wired around. They fed themselves whatever food they had until the military government came over and took over.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: You didn't have contact with them.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: We just spotted up the machine guns each and guns and made sure that they didn't - One time we were given an assignment to act as bridge guards to make sure that when they - the 12th Armored Division had captured a bridge across the Danube River down in Dillingen, Germany. We went down there and had to protect the bridge head from floating mines and stuff like that. At Nuremburg we were given, the company was given, an assignment to act as infantry troops. We had to clear out part Nuremburg, Germany. We had to go back and perform the duty of Rifle Company again. The company earned the Presidential Citation for what we did there. We did different things like that, all the way through until the end of the war. I, basically at that particular time, was out of fighting. When we crossed the Rhine River, we were given an assignment using our anti-tank guns at the time to help support the infantry crossing the river. The food I was eating - I thought about this, this morning - prior to this, while I was in the infantry we were eating C rations all the time. Which was, each meal consisted of two cans. One of them was biscuits - had three biscuits, hardtack, and pieces of candy, four cigarettes, and some sugar and so forth. The other can was your meal; meat and beans, vegetable stew, chicken, and dumplings. And that's what we had, or we had a four ounce chocolate bar. Which you couldn't bite into, and it wouldn't melt unless it was 170 degrees. And you use that as a ration, emergency ration. You see pictures of Germans passing out chocolate bars. Well, that was what they were. It was made of up of - it wasn't very good. It wouldn't melt. In order to eat it you had to chop it off with an axe. That was an emergency ration. When I transferred to the anti-tank company, because we had vehicles, we were supplied with what we called Ten-men Rations. There was a box of groceries that would feed ten men a day. It had chicken; it had bread; it had vegetables; it had fruit.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: You were eating like a king.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: Yeah, I was eating like king. My living conditions improved. Instead of sleeping outside in the rain and everything else. We'd move into a town or something like that, we'd commandeer a house. So, we had a house to live in and the bed to sleep in and so on.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: I've read about several - you received several medals from the french government. What did that mean to you? Was that an honor for you?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: Because of service to France, which was only awarded to people that had helped win the war for France, I was made a Chevalier in the French Legion of Honor, or a Knight in the French legion of Honor. The medal was designed by Napoleon. What it meant to me was that the French really appreciation what we did and they do. We went to Paris for our 60th wedding anniversary. Our son took us to Paris, and the Parisians treated us fine, excellent. Part of the reason is that they have very few elderly people in Paris, because they were all killed or taken away by the Germans. My wife - if we would get on the underground L train they would always give my wife a seat. When we asked questions, they would try to help us. Now prior to that time, when I was first over there, I had no desire to go back to Europe. My son said to my wife, "Do you want a party or do you want to go to Paris?" She picket Paris.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Of course, she picked Paris. When you did come home you, said you had changed so much. If you can talk about how you felt when you came home?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: I was older. I had seen so much. Everybody - most everybody that was - that didn't have the experiences I had, seemed so much younger. The only people I was comfortable with, you might say, was people my age. I don't know if I mentioned after I came back, I wanted to go back and finish school. And it took me several months, I'll use the word, to unwind. I don't - part of what wrong with the world today. My mother always used to tell me that when I came back, I would walk in - before I walked into a room, I would hesitate. Why? Because I was listening for stuff. And she'd say I used to take a sniff. Because being in battle your senses increase. Tremendously. I could hear a pin drop. I used to be able to see a leave in a tree blow when there was no wind. I my eyesight improved. You just - all five senses improve and in some cases you might say you acquire a sixth, but your five senses sharpen tremendously, and if you didn't use them. The chances were against you. You had to use your five senses and that was - and you had to train yourself to do it. It's something that nobody's going to tell you what to do. Everybody - every nationality smells different; they do. I used to be able to smell whenever the enemy was in the other room. I don't have the same - my senses aren't that sharp anymore.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: When you said that you felt death in that battleground, did anyone else experience it?

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: I don't know. I'm just saying that I was riding in the - I was being transported towards the front lines, and we moved through this battlefield, and I felt something. It was different; it was quiet. For one thing, there was a strange - there wasn't any breeze but yet there was. I was breathing air, but it wasn't the same air. Just different. And it was so quite it was just unbelievable, and something seemed to touch me. I felt the same thing in Dachau. There was all kinds of excitement going on in Dachau at the time and yet it was very, very quiet.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: That's the six sense you were talking about.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: I felt it, and when I went to the Holocaust Museum in DC. You walk into the building and the same quietness is there. And they have exhibits of the box cars that they used there, and they have exhibits of the clothes and shoes that people wore on display, and they had a display if a crematorium, the doors to the crematorium.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: It was chilling.

sp.speaker: Richard Koepke
sp.p: I've been to Holocaust Museum in Skokie. It's entirely different.

sp.speaker: Emily Lee
sp.p: Well, thank you sir. It was fascinating.
